proposal.utterance: An AI system can be the bearer of a juridical role.

entities.label: AISystem
entities.rationale: An AI system is a material entity: it has physical instantiation (hardware, software substrate) with mass and spatial extent, persisting through time. It is a kind (common noun), not a named individual.

entities.label: JuridicalRole
entities.rationale: A juridical role (e.g., legal person, party, rights-bearer) is a role in the BFO sense: externally grounded, inhering in a bearer, realized in legal processes. It is a kind (common noun). This is more specific than the existing LegalRight/LegalObligation classes which are also roles but represent specific normative positions rather than the general category of juridical roles.

relations.rationale: AISystem is a subclass of Material entity (BFO_0000040) as justified above.
JuridicalRole is a subclass of Role (BFO_0000023), externally grounded in legal-institutional context.
As a role, JuridicalRole is also a specifically dependent continuant (BFO_0000020), inhering in a bearer.

OWL axiom: AISystem subClassOf (bearer_of some JuridicalRole) — expresses that instances of AISystem can bear instances of JuridicalRole. This encodes the thesis as a subclass restriction using RO_0000053.

open_questions: Should 'AISystem' be restricted to software agents, or does it include embodied robotic systems as well? This affects whether BFO_0000040 (material entity) is the right top type, or whether a distinction between the physical system and the software information artifact (BFO_0000031) is needed.

Is the claim normative (AI systems *ought* to be able to bear juridical roles) or descriptive (some AI systems *do* in fact bear juridical roles in some legal system)? This affects whether we model this as a disposition (capacity) or an actual role instance.
Should JuridicalRole be modeled as a subclass of the existing working:LegalRight or working:CourtAuthority, or is it a more general superclass that those are subclasses of?

Is the intent to assert this as a general class-level axiom (all AI systems can bear juridical roles) or only that some AI systems can (existential restriction)? The former is a strong claim that may be controversial.
Does 'bearer' here mean the AI system itself is the legal subject (analogous to corporate personhood), or that it acts as an agent on behalf of a legal person? These are ontologically distinct.
proposal.rationale_summary: The utterance introduces two new kinds not previously in the ontology: AISystem (a material entity, BFO_0000040) and JuridicalRole (a role, BFO_0000023). proposal.utterance: Digital personhood is a legal status realized in institutional recognition.

entities.label: DigitalPersonhood
entities.rationale: Digital personhood is described as a legal status, which in BFO is best modeled as a Role (BFO_0000023): an externally grounded specifically dependent continuant that inheres in a bearer and is contingent on social/institutional context. It is analogous to existing working classes LegalRight and LegalObligation which are also typed as BFO_0000023.

entities.label: InstitutionalRecognitionProcess
entities.rationale: The utterance asserts that digital personhood (a role/realizable) is realized in institutional recognition. BFO_0000054 (realized in) links a realizable entity to a process. The existing class SocialRecognition (BFO_0000015) is close but pertains to social recognition generally; InstitutionalRecognitionProcess is a more specific subclass of Process capturing the institutional dimension of recognition events in which legal statuses are realized.

relations.rationale: Institutional recognition is a specific kind of social recognition process; making InstitutionalRecognitionProcess a subclass of the existing SocialRecognition class (BFO_0000015) preserves hierarchy and avoids duplication.
Digital personhood as a legal status is a species of legal right/role; subclassing under LegalRight (itself BFO_0000023) positions it correctly in the role hierarchy without asserting full identity.

The utterance explicitly states that digital personhood (a realizable entity) is realized in institutional recognition (a process). BFO_0000054 (realized in) is the canonical predicate for this relationship between a role/disposition and the process in which it manifests.

open_questions: Should DigitalPersonhood be typed more specifically as a subclass of LegalRight (an entitlement), LegalObligation, or a standalone Role class? The utterance says 'legal status' which could encompass both rights and obligations.

Is 'institutional recognition' here intended to refer to a specific type of legal act (e.g., legislative conferral, judicial determination) or a broader ongoing social process? This would affect whether InstitutionalRecognitionProcess should be further differentiated.

Should DigitalPersonhood be restricted to bearers that are digital agents or AI systems specifically, or does it also cover digital representations of natural persons and corporations? This would affect what bearer class is specified in a future restriction axiom.

Is there an intended individual (e.g., a specific jurisdiction's statute or court ruling) that confers digital personhood, which should be added as an individual of type InstitutionalRecognitionProcess or Statute?
proposal.rationale_summary: The utterance makes two ontological commitments: (1) digital personhood is a legal status, and (2) that status is realized in institutional recognition. In BFO, a legal status that is externally grounded, inheres in a bearer, and depends on social context is a Role (BFO_0000023). The realization relation BFO_0000054 (realized in) requires a Process as its range, so institutional recognition must be typed as BFO_0000015. The existing class SocialRecognition already captures social recognition processes, so InstitutionalRecognitionProcess is introduced as a subclass to capture the specifically institutional dimension. DigitalPersonhood is placed under LegalRight as the most closely matching existing role class, though this is flagged as an open question since 'legal status' may be broader. The three proposed relations encode the subclass hierarchy and the realization link asserted by the utterance.

proposal.utterance: A smart contract encodes obligations as executable patterns.

entities.label: SmartContract
entities.rationale: A smart contract is an information artifact — an encoded pattern of conditional instructions — that can be copied, instantiated on different platforms, and whose content is what carries the normative and computational force. It is a generically dependent continuant because its identity is tied to its pattern/content, not a single bearer.

entities.label: ExecutableObligation
entities.rationale: An executable obligation is an obligation encoded as a computable pattern within a smart contract. The obligation's normative content is represented as an information structure (generically dependent continuant), distinct from the dispositional or role-based obligation borne by a specific agent. This distinguishes the encoded representation from any instantiated legal obligation (working:LegalObligation, a role/SDC).

entities.label: EncodingProcess
entities.rationale: The act of encoding obligations into executable patterns is a process — it unfolds in time and results in a smart contract bearing encoded obligations. Modeled as a BFO Process subclass.

relations.rationale: An executable obligation is a specialization of the broader legal obligation concept already in the ontology, restricting to those whose content is encoded as a computable pattern. NOTE: this asserts a subclass relation between a GDC subclass (ExecutableObligation as encoded content) and LegalObligation (typed as BFO_0000023/Role). This may cause a type-clash since LegalObligation is an SDC/Role and ExecutableObligation is proposed as GDC. Flagged in open_questions.

A smart contract has as part (or concretely: as a constituent information component) one or more executable obligations encoded within it. BFO_0000051 (has part) is appropriate for GDC-to-GDC part relations.
The encoding process has as participant the smart contract that results from or is the output of the encoding.

open_questions: Should ExecutableObligation be typed as a GDC (encoded pattern) rather than subclassing working:LegalObligation (an SDC/Role)? If so, the subClassOf relation to LegalObligation should be dropped or replaced with a cross-category bridge relation (e.g., 'is encoded representation of').

Is a SmartContract best treated purely as a GDC (information pattern), or does it also have a material instantiation (e.g., deployed bytecode on a blockchain node) that warrants a material entity component? Should we model both the abstract content (GDC) and the concrete instantiation (material)?

Does 'encodes' refer to a temporal process of authoring, or to a standing structural relation between the smart contract and the obligation? If the latter, should we mint a custom object property 'encodes' rather than using BFO_0000051 (has part)?

Are the obligations encoded in smart contracts meant to be the same kind as working:LegalObligation (legally binding roles), or merely computational representations of obligation-like constraints (which may or may not have legal force)?
proposal.rationale_summary: The utterance asserts that a smart contract (a kind of information artifact) encodes obligations as executable patterns. In BFO terms, the smart contract is naturally a generically dependent continuant — its identity is its encoded content, copyable across platforms. The obligations-as-encoded-patterns are likewise GDCs: they are information structures representing normative constraints in computable form. The encoding itself is a process. The main ontological tension is between working:LegalObligation (already typed as a role/SDC inhering in a bearer) and ExecutableObligation (proposed as a GDC — the encoded representation). These are distinct ontological kinds: one is the normative status borne by an agent, the other is an information artifact encoding that content. A subClassOf link between them risks a BFO type clash and is flagged for user clarification. The has-part relation between SmartContract and ExecutableObligation is provisionally used but a dedicated 'encodes' property may be more semantically precise.

proposal.utterance: An autonomous agent participates in processes of recognition without consciousness.

entities.label: AutonomousAgent
entities.rationale: An autonomous agent is a material entity (has mass and spatial extension) capable of acting in processes without requiring consciousness. Typed as Material entity because agents that participate in processes must be continuants with physical instantiation in BFO. The utterance does not specify a specific individual, so this is a class.

entities.label: NonConsciousRecognitionProcess
entities.rationale: A recognition process that unfolds in time and does not require a conscious bearer. The utterance asserts that recognition can occur without consciousness, motivating a subtype of Process distinct from existing SocialRecognition (which implies social/human agents). This class captures autonomous/non-conscious recognition as a process kind.

entities.label: Consciousness
entities.rationale: Consciousness is an internally grounded capacity (disposition) of certain material entities. The utterance asserts its absence in autonomous agents, so it must be represented to capture the negation. Typed as Disposition because consciousness is a capacity or potentiality that inheres in a bearer and may or may not be realized.

relations.rationale: NonConsciousRecognitionProcess is a subtype of the existing SocialRecognition process class, specializing it to cases where the participating agent lacks consciousness.
AutonomousAgent participates in (RO_0000056) NonConsciousRecognitionProcess, as asserted by the utterance that autonomous agents participate in recognition processes.

Consciousness as a disposition inheres in (RO_0000052) a bearer; here the relation is used as a schema-level axiom on the class. The utterance asserts autonomous agents lack this disposition, but the disposition class must be represented for the negation to be assertable. A subclass axiom or complement restriction could later encode its absence.

open_questions: Should 'AutonomousAgent' be restricted to artificial/computational agents (e.g., AI systems, robots), or does it include any agent lacking consciousness (e.g., simple organisms)? This affects the parent class choice and any disjointness axioms.

Is 'NonConsciousRecognitionProcess' meant to be a strict subclass of SocialRecognition, or should it be a sibling? Social recognition typically presupposes social actors; an autonomous agent's recognition may be merely functional rather than social.

Should we assert that AutonomousAgent bearers are necessarily NOT bearers of Consciousness (i.e., encode the negation as a disjointness or complement restriction)? This requires OWL negation (owl:complementOf) and should be confirmed before adding.

Is 'autonomous agent' here intended to be a BFO Material entity (e.g., a physical robot), or could it also encompass abstract computational processes (which might better fit as a Process or a role-bearing entity)?
proposal.rationale_summary: The utterance introduces three new ontological commitments: (1) a kind of agent—AutonomousAgent—that is a material entity capable of acting without consciousness; (2) a kind of process—NonConsciousRecognitionProcess—that is a subtype of the existing SocialRecognition process, occurring without a conscious participant; and (3) Consciousness as a disposition class that inheres in material entities, whose absence in AutonomousAgent is the key claim. The participation relation (RO_0000056) links AutonomousAgent to NonConsciousRecognitionProcess. The absence of consciousness is noted but cannot be formally encoded without OWL complement axioms, which are flagged as an open question. No existing individuals from the working ontology are reused, but the existing SocialRecognition class is used as parent for the new process class.

proposal.utterance: Algorithmic accountability depends on the traceability of computational processes.

entities.label: AlgorithmicAccountability
entities.rationale: Algorithmic accountability is an internally grounded capacity or normative requirement that a system or agent has to answer for the behavior of algorithms. It is dispositional: it is a real capacity that may or may not be realized in auditing or oversight processes. BFO Disposition fits because it is grounded in the nature of the bearer (the computational system or institution).

entities.label: ComputationalProcess
entities.rationale: A computational process is an occurrent that unfolds in time and involves computational operations. It is straightforwardly a BFO Process.

entities.label: Traceability
entities.rationale: Traceability is a measurable property that inheres in a computational process or system: the degree to which its steps, inputs, outputs, and decision paths can be followed and reconstructed. It is a Quality (BFO_0000019) of the process or the system bearing it.

entities.label: AccountabilityRealizingProcess
entities.rationale: The process in which algorithmic accountability is realized (e.g., an audit, an investigation, a review). Needed to ground the BFO_0000054 (realized in) relation from AlgorithmicAccountability to a process type.

relations.rationale: Traceability is typed as a subclass of Quality (BFO_0000019), inhering in computational processes or systems.
AlgorithmicAccountability is typed as a Disposition, a subclass of BFO_0000016.
ComputationalProcess is a subclass of Process (BFO_0000015).
AccountabilityRealizingProcess is a subclass of Process (BFO_0000015).
Algorithmic accountability as a disposition is realized in accountability processes such as audits and oversight procedures.
Traceability inheres in computational processes; it is a quality of those processes.

The claim that accountability depends on traceability is captured by asserting that AlgorithmicAccountability (as a disposition class) has a necessary precondition in the presence of Traceability quality in the relevant ComputationalProcess. This is expressed as an OWL axiom: AlgorithmicAccountability realized in AccountabilityRealizingProcess which has participant ComputationalProcess which bears Traceability.

open_questions: Should 'AlgorithmicAccountability' be modeled as a Disposition (internally grounded capacity of a system/institution) or as a Role (externally conferred social obligation)? The distinction matters: if it is an externally imposed legal or social requirement, BFO_0000023 (Role) may be more appropriate.

What is the primary bearer of AlgorithmicAccountability — a software system (Material entity), an organization (Legal institution), or an individual agent? This determines where the disposition inheres.

Should 'Traceability' be a Quality of the ComputationalProcess itself, or of the computational system (material entity) that executes the process? BFO requires qualities to inhere in a specific bearer.

Is 'depends on' here meant as a strict ontological necessary condition (the disposition cannot be realized without traceability), or a weaker epistemic condition (traceability enables evaluation of accountability)? The former justifies a stronger OWL axiom; the latter may only warrant an annotation.

Should we also represent 'algorithmic system' or 'algorithm' as an entity class (likely BFO_0000031 Generically Dependent Continuant for the algorithm as information content, and BFO_0000040 for the hardware)?
proposal.rationale_summary: The utterance asserts a dependency relation between two concepts: algorithmic accountability and traceability of computational processes. In BFO terms, algorithmic accountability is best typed as a Disposition (BFO_0000016) — an internally grounded capacity or normative requirement inhering in some bearer (a system, institution, or agent) that is realized in oversight or auditing processes. Traceability is a Quality (BFO_0000019) that inheres in computational processes, representing the degree to which those processes can be followed and reconstructed. The dependency claim — that accountability depends on traceability — is represented structurally: the AccountabilityRealizingProcess (in which AlgorithmicAccountability is realized) has as participant a ComputationalProcess, and that ComputationalProcess bears a Traceability quality. This encodes the dependence without conflating the process with the disposition. Four new classes are minted; no existing working ontology entities are directly reusable, though the new entities are consistent with the existing LegalInstitution, BehavioralLegalManifestation, and InstitutionalFunction classes in the graph.
